attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: Present-tense observation listing three problems as examples. The normalisation keeps the scope. Wolfram Alpha is given only as an example.

contract.note: The plain reading (problems persisted in leading LLMs, not every model failing every task) is ordinary and fair. Using 2023 through publication as the window is reasonable.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own GPT-4 disclosure admits it still hallucinates. This is a company disclosure but an admission against its interest. It also reports progress.
API-Bank preprint from before the post documents substantial tool-use failures. It is not a Wolfram Alpha test.
The v2 revision, available before the post, shows large behaviour changes between the March and June versions of GPT-3.5/4.
OpenAI let developers pin versions but admitted regressions across upgrades. This qualifies the engineering implication without contradicting it.

reviews.rationale: Evidence from before the post meets every part of the support condition: OpenAI admits ongoing hallucination, a benchmark records material tool-use failures, and a study shows big changes between the March and June versions. Version pinning and reported improvements qualify the instability point but do not show the problems were solved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words. He relays a rumour but presents it as his own observation.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'rumored' qualifier as 'reportedly'. Marcus named no reporting period and no industry boundary.

contract.note: Testing realized aggregate revenue for one quarter (April-June 2023) is the evaluator's choice. An ordinary reader would take 'current revenues' as an annual scale. The quarterly window is stretched and decides whether the threshold is met.

evidence.note: OpenAI alone, and a forecast ($200M for 2023) plus a later run rate. It is not realized industry revenue for the target quarter.
Bloomberg Intelligence forecast of a trillion-dollar market by 2032. Its market definition includes hardware, so it is a different metric, and it does not show what any valuation assumed.

reviews.rationale: Neither item measures aggregate generative-AI revenue on a comparable basis, and nothing ties specific valuations to trillion-dollar market assumptions. The result also depends on a reporting interval the evaluator chose. The packet does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The firm forecast is continued undergraduate use. The open-source shift is hedged ('most likely'), so it is not scored. 'Pockets aren't deep' is a background observation.

contract.note: The support condition and the early-resolution rule both depend on the hedged open-source migration. Under policy that part is not scored, so the firm continued-use forecast should have been assessed on its own.

evidence.note: HEPI survey (fieldwork December 2025, UK undergraduates) finds near-universal generative AI use. This fits continued use, but in one country only.
Institution-provided tools are mostly ChatGPT and Copilot. That is institutional provision, not a measure of students switching.

reviews.rationale: The open-source part is hedged, so it is not adjudicable. The firm continued-use forecast has no deadline. Undergraduates were still using generative AI as of December 2025, but with an open horizon and no conclusive event under the contract's rule, the forecast cannot be finally scored.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Helped only partially' fairly renders 'helped in some ways, but not others'. The 'cannot guarantee' scope is kept.

contract.note: Reading 'guarantee' as general behavioural assurance, with the listed bad behaviours as examples, is an ordinary and fair plain reading.

evidence.note: Inverse-scaling preprint from before the post: some tasks get worse with scale, alongside general gains, with noted exceptions.
Llama 2 paper (Meta's own disclosure) admits harmful or biased outputs may remain after mitigation, plus hallucination.
Anthropic reports gains for Claude 2. This supports 'helped in some ways' but does not isolate scale or show any guarantee.

reviews.rationale: Contemporary scaling research shows uneven gains, with some tasks worsening as models grow. Model documentation admits harmful, biased and hallucinated outputs remain. Nothing in the packet shows dependable assurance. Reported capability gains match the 'helped in some ways' part.
